conditions.1_question: Holds. Both predict MCI-to-AD progression in ADNI MCI participants (P-81 ADNI-1/2/GO; P-88 ADNI-2/GO) from baseline FDG-PET alone, which is the PET channel in both. Horizon (within 3 years vs during up to 8 years of follow-up) and PET representation (whole-brain 3D CNN vs a 10-feature white-matter radiomics signature) are allowed differences.
conditions.3_matched_figure: Holds. Neither paper reports the other's condition: P-88 has no 3-year result and no whole-brain model; P-81 has no radiomics signature and no longer horizon. The cognitive-score arms agree (0.750 vs 0.742), but they are a different quantity (clinical channel), not the PET arm under the other paper's condition, so they do not reconcile the PET gap.
conditions.4_uncertainty: Holds in one direction, robustly. P-81 reports mean +- fold SD, not an interval, so Hanley-McNeil applies: 93 pMCI / 164 sMCI gives SE 0.0372 and [0.537, 0.683]; if only the 85% train+validation pool (79/139) entered the folds, [0.531, 0.689]. P-88's test AUC 0.719 lies outside both. The exclusion does not depend on the interval construction: a logit-scale interval from the same SE gives [0.535, 0.680] (or [0.529, 0.686]), and P-81's own fold dispersion gives 0.6102 + 1.96 x 0.0231 = 0.655 even if the fold SD were treated as the SE of one fold. The reverse does not hold: P-88's [0.605, 0.833] (31/72) contains 0.610. Two-sample z = 1.58. The rule asks for one estimate outside the other's interval, and C-121, C-82 and C-83 were qualified, and upheld on skeptic review, on exactly this one-directional pattern (C-121 with z = 1.17 and 1.81).
conditions.5_performance_validity: Holds. No conversion AUC is near 0.97. P-81's 1.0 values are its CN-vs-AD pretraining (Table 2), not the compared quantity.
conditions.6_record: The record misreads P-88 (it prints 0.719 test / 0.747 training, not 0.79) and frames the pair as an ordering dispute that dissolves on the printed figures. Condition 6 directs judging the figures the papers print. The PET-alone conversion AUC is the record's own claim_b quantity, and P-81 prints the same quantity (PET ONLY). Judging a pair on a printed shared quantity rather than the misread one is how C-67 (qualified on AD vs MCI, a contrast the record never named), C-12, C-46, C-69 and C-82 were read. The reader's reservation that the gap 'sits on a quantity the record did not dispute' is therefore not a ground under the rule.

figures.P-88: Psychoradiomics (white-matter FDG-PET) signature, test group (72 stable / 31 progressive, split by ADNI entry number): AUC 0.719, no interval printed (text, Table 3 and Fig. 3B). Hanley-McNeil 31/72: Q1 = 0.5613, Q2 = 0.6015, SE^2 = 7.532/2232 = 0.00337, SE 0.0581, [0.605, 0.833]. Training AUC 0.747 (apparent, on the group used to select the features). ADAS 0.742 [0.631, 0.853]; CDR 0.737.

results.reason: Every condition holds on the sources. The recorded ordering dispute dissolves, but condition 6 sends the pair to the figures the papers print, and on the shared PET-alone conversion AUC P-88's 0.719 lies outside P-81's derived interval [0.537, 0.683] under every construction tried (full or 85% n, Wald or logit, or P-81's own fold spread). The exclusion is one-directional (z = 1.58), which the rule accepts and which C-121, C-82 and C-83 were qualified on. The candidate explanations (horizon, zero-shot whole-brain CNN vs white-matter radiomics, validation design, ADNI phases) are not shown by either paper to be sufficient.

conditions.1_question: Holds. MCI vs cognitively normal classification from T1 structural MRI in ADNI older adults (P-109 3T subset; P-66 1.5T subset).
conditions.2_metric: Holds. Accuracy with accuracy and AUC with AUC.
conditions.3_matched_figure: Holds. P-109 has no ROI, 1.5T or subject-level result; P-66 has no whole-brain result. Every P-109 model on its own split (Table 4, MCI/HC 85.13-94.23%, AUC 0.934-0.972) stays outside P-66's interval, so no figure in either paper closes the gap. A different architecture on P-109's split is not P-66's condition.
conditions.4_uncertainty: Holds in both directions under every n. P-109 94.23% at the most conservative n = 69 test subjects: Wilson [0.861, 0.977]; P-66's 72.7% lies outside. P-66 at its most conservative n (20% test partition, about 80 subjects): [0.621, 0.813]; at n = 400, [0.681, 0.768]; 94.23% lies outside both. AUC: P-109 0.9715, Hanley-McNeil 37/32 [0.932, 1.0]; P-66 0.80 at 40/40 [0.702, 0.898] or 200/200 [0.757, 0.843]; each estimate lies outside the other's interval.
conditions.5_performance_validity: Holds on the letter, checked against the source. The declared exclusion (Section 2) is conjunctive: 'near-ceiling discrimination on internal validation with small samples (at or above 0.97 accuracy or AUC, no external cohort)'. P-109 meets the ceiling clause (MCI/HC AUC 0.9715, AD/HC 0.9852 and 97.13%), internal validation and no external cohort, but not the small-sample clause: 1,075 participants, 685 in the MCI/HC contrast. That is larger than every study Section 3.5 names as its exemplars (P-200 582, P-1 383, P-197 125, P-119 unreported), which the review itself describes as 'small-to-modest samples'. The same reading was applied to the same paper and the same AUCs in C-46 (qualified yes) and upheld on skeptic review ('It does not meet the third, a small sample ... P-109 is not in the suspect set'); C-68 and C-84 read it the same way. The shuffled-slice split is the mechanism Section 3.5 names as a candidate, but the exclusion as declared contains no split-unit clause, so it enters as the leading candidate explanation, not as a failed condition. Against this reading: P-109 itself says it used 'only a small amount of ADNI Alzheimer's data', and the review sets no numeric cut-off for 'small' (as C-194 notes). That phrase concerns data volume for deep learning, not the review's criterion, and applying a looser reading here but not in C-46 would break the brief's requirement that every candidate be judged identically. P-66 passes (at most AUC 0.90).
conditions.6_record: The record's comparison (three-class 96.81% vs an '~82%' P-66 does not print) is a misreading; the pair is judged on the MCI vs CN figures both papers print, as in C-46, C-83 and C-84.

conditions.1_question: Holds, on both prongs the reader left open. Task: both discriminate AACD-defined MCI (score at least 1 SD below the age-band mean) from non-MCI among Chinese older adults in CHARLS with a random forest on routine tabular data. (a) Population class. P-27's sample is CHARLS 2018 respondents aged 60+ whose CESD-10 score is 10 or more; P-96's is CHARLS 2015 older adults (mean age 70.7) with no depression-based selection stated and no depression variable among its 34 candidates. P-27's sample is therefore a symptom-screen subset of the community population P-96 samples, drawn from the same national survey, not a separate disease population. That is the distinction the round drew in C-180/C-181, which failed condition 1 because diabetic inpatients and dust-exposed miners are populations of different kinds and 'Neither sample is a subset of the other's population', and it matches C-214 (early-MCI subset, qualified) and C-265 (family-history-enriched cohort vs a random community sample, qualified). The depression restriction is a cohort difference, which the rule allows as a candidate explanation. (b) Channel. The rule's channel is 'clinical/cognitive/questionnaire data', and a multimodal model matches when the compared channel is shared. P-96 describes its predictors as 'basic clinical indicators' drawn from demographics, health conditions, lifestyle, physical examination and blood tests; its model adds grip strength (motor) and routine blood values (fluid) to demographic and anthropometric clinical data. The shared clinical channel carries each model's top predictor: education is P-96's most influential SHAP feature and first in P-27's SHAP list. Unimodal-vs-multimodal pairs sharing a channel were qualified in C-103 and C-188. Against: P-96 contrasts itself with studies that 'use baseline MMSE score and other questionnaire data'; that marks the absence of cognitive tests among its inputs, not a different channel under the rule's list.
conditions.3_matched_figure: Holds. Neither paper reports the other's population subset (no depressed subgroup in P-96, no non-depressed sample in P-27). The closest matched figure makes the gap wider: P-27's CLHLS external validation labels MCI with the CMMSE, the same MMSE-type AACD label P-96 uses, and it gives 0.653, against P-96's 0.83 and 0.87. At every validation tier the gap persists.
conditions.4_uncertainty: Holds in both directions on reported intervals at every tier. Development: 0.826 [0.809, 0.843] vs 0.93 [0.91, 0.95]. P-27 internal hold-out 0.801 [0.760, 0.841] and 5-fold CV 0.791 [0.771, 0.810] vs 0.93 [0.91, 0.95]. External: 0.653 [0.636, 0.670] vs 0.83 [0.82, 0.84] and 0.87 [0.86, 0.88]. The reported intervals match Hanley-McNeil (P-27 external 1146/5636 [0.635, 0.671]; P-96 External Set 1 572/3568 [0.809, 0.851]), so they are sample intervals, and none overlaps.
conditions.5_performance_validity: Holds. Maximum 0.93; both papers validate externally.
conditions.6_record: Holds. The record's 0.826 and 0.93 are printed development-set values, and the gap is confirmed on the external figures.

candidate_explanations.difference: P-96's threshold metrics imply class-balanced evaluation sets at every tier although its text says SMOTE was not applied to test or external sets: External Set 1 PPV 0.735 at sensitivity 0.782 and specificity 0.718 corresponds to 50% prevalence (at the stated 13.8% it would be 0.307); External Set 2 PPV 0.793 likewise (0.436 expected at 16.7%). If AUROCs were computed on resampled sets they could be optimistic. AUROC does not depend on class balance as such, so this is not shown to close the gap.
candidate_explanations.quote: SMOTE was performed exclusively within the training folds during cross-validation and was not applied to test sets or external validation cohorts.

candidate_explanations.difference: Different CHARLS waves (2018 vs 2015 and 2011) with likely participant overlap, so the samples are not independent.

results.reason: Conditions 2 to 6 hold on reported intervals at every tier, and the closest label-matched figure (P-27's CMMSE-labelled external 0.653) widens the gap. Condition 1 also holds: P-27's depressed sample is a symptom-screen subset of the same CHARLS community population P-96 samples (the subset relation that separates this pair from C-180/C-181 and aligns it with C-214 and C-265), and both models are routine clinical tabular models whose top predictor is education, with P-96's grip strength and blood values as added channels under the multimodal clause. The depression restriction, predictor sets, label instrument, external cohorts and P-96's apparently balanced evaluation sets are candidate explanations, none shown to be sufficient.

conditions.1_question: Holds. Three-year MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI from baseline structural MRI; P-72's sMRI-only arm is P-37's input condition.
conditions.2_metric: Holds. Accuracy and AUC are both printed for the conversion task.
conditions.3_matched_figure: Fails on the metric the record disputes. P-72's sMRI-only MAResNet18 arm is the matched figure (same horizon, same single-timepoint MRI input). Its accuracy 73.68% lies inside P-37's [0.716, 0.896], and P-37's 82.4% lies inside the arm's [0.610, 0.834] at n = 57, so the papers' own data dissolve the accuracy gap. The strongest counter I found: the rule's n is 'subjects in the test set', P-72 averages three 'different test sets', and if their union reached 75 subjects P-37's 82.4% would fall outside the arm's interval. The paper does not say the sets are disjoint, and its own spread argues against pooling: the multimodal model's SD across the three splits is 1.01 points, against about 5.6 points expected from independent 57-subject test sets (inference, not stated in the paper). P-72's headline multimodal model agrees with P-37 in both directions on both metrics.
conditions.4_uncertainty: Not established. On AUC the matched arm's 0.721 lies 0.008 below P-37's Wald Hanley-McNeil bound 0.729 (37/31; 0.725 with class roles swapped), while 0.827 lies inside the arm's [0.580, 0.862]; z = 1.21. The separation does not survive a logit-scale interval built from the same Hanley-McNeil SE (P-37 [0.707, 0.904], which contains 0.721), so it depends on an interval-construction choice the rule does not fix. By contrast, C-07's one-directional exclusion holds under both constructions. This is the strongest case for qualification, and it is not robust enough to meet condition 4 on the sources.
conditions.5_performance_validity: Holds. No conversion figure is near ceiling; P-72's 94.61% is AD vs NC.
conditions.6_record: The recorded 94.61% is P-72's AD vs NC accuracy; judged on the printed conversion figures, which reverse the recorded direction.

Multimodal SPDFC(0.6): 77.19% (SD 1.01 over the three splits), AUC 0.755 [0.620, 0.890].

results.reason: The advocate case rests on the AUC of P-72's sMRI-only arm, which falls 0.008 below P-37's Wald Hanley-McNeil bound in one direction only. That separation disappears under a logit-scale interval from the same SE. The same matched arm's accuracy, which is the metric the record disputes, agrees with P-37 within uncertainty in both directions at the test-set size the paper supports. So the papers' own matched data dissolve the recorded gap (condition 3), and the residual AUC difference is not shown to be beyond uncertainty (condition 4). It would change only if P-72 showed that its three test sets are disjoint (n = 171). Then accuracy would clear in one direction and AUC in both.
